_comment: A socket is one physical opening. Joints that sit at the same point are
the same opening described more than once -- because a joint can hold only
one layer and one facing, so a post that takes either a scope or a wheel
needs two joints, and a mount that allows two facings needs two more.
Nothing in the catalog accepts two parts at one spot, so proximity is the
whole rule and there is no exclusion table here. Keep it that way: if two
joints share a point but are really different openings, the fix belongs in
marker_offsets or in the model, not in a list of exceptions.
_cluster_epsilon_note: Joints closer than this are one opening. Chosen from the measured gap in
the data: the widest pair that must merge is scope/wheel at 0.084, and the
nearest pair that must NOT merge is a tower's centre-vs-rail alternatives
at 0.296. Anything from 0.09 to 0.29 gives the same answer.
_default_fittings_note: Toys a tower arrives with. Fitted when one is placed, and removable like
anything else -- deleting one takes only that one.
`mount` is the joint each toy was modelled for. Scope and wheel mounts are
one layer now, but they are not interchangeable in the model: on the DX
Play Tower the scope mount on a side faces one way and the wheel mount on
the same side faces the other, so a wheel fitted to a scope mount comes out
backwards. The joint names still say which is which -- merging the layers
moved the old name into the prefix rather than dropping it -- so each toy
goes on the mount built for it.
`prefer` breaks ties where a tower has several of the right mount: the
scope takes the highest, the wheel the lowest, which is how the towers with
two rows were drawn. Where neither mount matches, any free point is used.
Only on placement. Restoring a saved design does not go through this path,
so opening a catalogue set gets what the set says and nothing more.
_layer_renames_note: Layers that turned out to be one thing under several names, renamed
A tower post took a Super Scope, the mount below it took a Steering Wheel
or Ship's Wheel, and a separate mount took a Mailbox or Telephone -- three
layer names for what Weldon confirms is one kind of fitting. Any of the
five toys now goes on any of them.
Applied to every model that carries these, so it holds for the towers and
for the toys themselves: 63 joints across 12 products become one layer.
Nothing special-cases a particular tower, which is the point -- a new toy
needs the 'toy' layer and nothing else.
_remove_joints_note: Connection points the models offer but the product does not.
Applied by tools/set_joint_layers.js, which renames the node rather than
deleting it: the app treats a node as a joint only if its name begins with
'joint', so a prefix takes it out of the system entirely. Deleting the node
would mean renumbering every index in the file's node graph for no gain,
and this way the original name is still legible and the change reversible.
P-ST: the Summit Tower offered a mailbox or telephone mount on each side.
Weldon asked for both to come out. Sky Tower keeps its pair, and no shipped
catalog set used the Summit ones.
P-KT: the King's Tower mailbox mounts, the pair up at the top corners.
Weldon asked for that point to go and it is the highest toy point on the
tower, which is why the Super Scope kept landing on it. The tower keeps a
scope mount and a wheel mount on each end face, and those still take any
of the five toys.
SR-KT: the Safety Rail's second plug, on layer '0'. That layer had exactly
one host in the catalog -- the King's Tower point just above -- so taking
that point out left this plug with nothing anywhere it could mate. The
rail still fits, through its 'end_rail' joint, which is how it goes on
every other tower. Removing it retires the layer as well: '0' is no longer
declared by anything.
P-KT also loses both ground-level points on its railed end. That end comes
with a picket panel built into the model -- the boards sit at z -1.24,
centred 0.471 up -- and the two points there offered a Side Rail and a
Kitchen Kit on top of the rail that is already standing. The open end keeps
its point, so both parts can still be fitted, on the end that has room for
them. The two are one opening each, so the Kitchen shares the lower point
with the Side Rail and goes with it.
Identify a joint by where it is, not by what it is called. This entry read
'joint_scope,0/2,toy' first, on the assumption that the point the scope
occupied was a scope mount. It was not: on this tower the scope joints sit
7cm from the wheel joints down on the end faces -- one socket, so removing
them deleted no dot at all -- while the point in question is a mailbox
mount 20cm higher at a corner.
_layer_overrides_note: Applied to the model files themselves by tools/set_joint_layers.js, because
the app parses a joint's layer out of the GLB at run time -- unlike marker
offsets and cut-outs, this cannot be corrected in the manifest.
These four carried '*', which matches EVERY socket in the catalog: a Bridge
could be hung off a swing hanger. Bridge and Tunnel span between decks, the
Bubble Panel goes wherever a climb goes, and Tic-Tac-Toe wherever a slide
goes -- all deck parts. 'deck' matches any deck height (5 = 4ft, 6 = 5ft,
8 = 7ft) and nothing else, which is a narrow rule in place of a wildcard.
BNS, the Bird's Nest Swing, is a different kind of correction. It plugged
with 's' like every other swing, so it hung from any hanger on any beam.
Weldon says it goes only at the opening closest to the beam's legs -- the
same one the Horse Glider takes. That opening is already the only one
carrying 'sh', on all six beams: the tower mount is at the far end and the
'sh' hanger sits at 0.96, furthest from it. So the layer already existed
and said the right thing; the Bird's Nest simply was not on it.
This is also the answer to whether 's' and 'sh' should merge: they should
not. 'sh' is not a second name for a swing hanger, it is the end position,
and two products in the catalog are sold only for it.
_default_yaw_note: Which way a free-standing model faces when first placed, in degrees, for
the few modelled facing a different way from the rest.
The Summit Tower and King's Tower were exported a quarter turn from the
other five, and were recognised by reading the name of the mesh inside the
GLB -- a match on 'King' or 'summitglb'. That works until one of them is
re-exported and the object comes out named something else, at which point
the tower silently places facing the wrong way. Keyed on the product id
instead, which does not change when a model is rebuilt.
The comment on the old test named the Watchtower, which was never one of
the two: its mesh is 'Watch_tower' and it matched neither string.
_cutouts_note: How much of a host's railing a part removes, for parts whose joint is a
bare empty and so carves nothing.
Slides and climbers carry this as geometry on the joint itself, and the
fence code hides any slat that box touches. Toys correctly carry none --
they mount on a rail rather than replacing it. Tic-Tac-Toe was authored
like a toy but goes where a slide goes, so every slat stayed standing.
It takes the Wave Slide's box exactly.
Declared here rather than added to the GLB: giving a node geometry means
writing accessors and buffer bytes, where this is one line and readable.
_marker_offsets_note: Where to DRAW a socket's dot, when that differs from where the part
attaches. Placement is untouched -- only the marker moves.
picnic: the table mounts to the posts above the floor, but its joint was
authored down at floor height, so its dot landed on top of the floor kit's.
The table itself is correctly placed, so the joint stays and the dot rises
